q: A company sells equipment, installation and a two-year service plan to a customer for a single price of $100,000. The standalone selling prices are equipment $80,000, installation $10,000 and service plan $30,000. Each is a distinct performance obligation. How much of the transaction price is allocated to the equipment?
exp: ASC 606 allocates the transaction price on a relative standalone selling price basis: $100,000 x ($80,000 / $120,000) = $66,667. Allocating the full $80,000 standalone price ignores the $20,000 bundle discount, which is spread across all obligations.

q: A contractor agrees to build a facility for $500,000 and will receive a $60,000 bonus if the facility is completed by a specified date. The contractor estimates a 70% probability of earning the bonus. Assume the variable consideration constraint does not limit the estimate. What transaction price should the contractor use?
exp: With only two possible outcomes, the most likely amount method best predicts the consideration, so the bonus is included in full: $500,000 + $60,000 = $560,000. The expected value method ($500,000 + 70% x $60,000 = $542,000) is the trap; it suits contracts with many possible outcomes.

q: A company with many similar contracts agrees to provide services for $50,000, subject to late-delivery penalties. Based on experience, it estimates a 50% chance of no penalty, a 30% chance of a $5,000 penalty and a 20% chance of a $10,000 penalty. Assume the constraint does not apply. Using the method that best predicts the consideration, what is the transaction price?
exp: With a range of outcomes and many similar contracts, the expected value method is appropriate: expected penalty = (30% x $5,000) + (20% x $10,000) = $3,500, so the price is $50,000 - $3,500 = $46,500. Using the most likely outcome of no penalty gives the $50,000 trap.

q: A retailer sells 1,000 units at $50 each (cost $30 each) with a right of return. Based on reliable experience, it expects 5% of units to be returned. How much revenue should the retailer recognize at the time of sale?
exp: Under ASC 606, revenue excludes expected returns: 950 units x $50 = $47,500, with a $2,500 refund liability and a $1,500 asset for the right to recover goods (50 x $30). Recognizing the full $50,000 ignores the variable consideration from returns.

q: An online travel company collects $200 from a customer for a hotel room and remits $170 to the hotel. The travel company never controls the room, and the hotel is responsible for providing it. How much revenue should the travel company recognize?
choices: $0, because no service is performed
exp: Because the company does not control the room before it is transferred, it is an agent and recognizes revenue net, equal to its $30 commission (ASC 606-10-55-36 through 55-40). Reporting $200 gross is the principal treatment, which does not apply here.

q: A contractor has a $3,000,000 fixed-price contract and recognizes revenue over time using the cost-to-cost input method. In Year 1, it incurred costs of $600,000 and estimates additional costs to complete of $1,800,000. How much revenue should it recognize in Year 1?
exp: Progress = $600,000 / ($600,000 + $1,800,000) = 25%, so revenue = 25% x $3,000,000 = $750,000. Dividing costs incurred by only the remaining costs ($600,000 / $1,800,000) produces the $1,000,000 trap, and $150,000 is the gross profit.

q: A contractor has a $2,000,000 fixed-price contract recognized over time. At the end of Year 1, costs incurred are $900,000 and estimated costs to complete are $1,300,000. What loss should the contractor recognize on the contract in Year 1?
exp: Total estimated cost of $2,200,000 exceeds the $2,000,000 price, and the entire expected loss of $200,000 must be recognized as soon as it is anticipated (ASC 605-35). Recognizing only the portion tied to progress ($900,000 / $2,200,000 x $200,000 = $81,818) is the trap.

q: On January 1, Year 1, a company delivers equipment to a customer who will pay $121,000 on December 31, Year 2. The cash selling price of the equipment is $100,000, reflecting a 10% annual financing rate. Control transfers on delivery. How much revenue from the sale of equipment is recognized on January 1, Year 1?
choices: $0 until cash is collected
exp: A significant financing component exists, so revenue is recognized at the cash selling price of $100,000 and the $21,000 difference is interest income over two years ($10,000 in Year 1). Recognizing $121,000 ignores the financing component.

q: A company paid a $20,000 commission to a salesperson for signing a four-year service contract, paid $3,000 in travel costs to make the sales pitch, and incurred $2,000 of legal fees to draft the contract that would have been incurred even if the contract had not been signed. How much should be capitalized as an incremental cost of obtaining the contract?
exp: Under ASC 340-40, only costs incurred because the contract was obtained, such as the $20,000 commission, are capitalized and amortized over the four-year term. Travel and legal costs incurred regardless of whether the contract is obtained are expensed, so $25,000 overstates the asset.

q: A manufacturer sells appliances with a standard 90-day warranty that the products will work as specified, and customers may also buy a separately priced three-year extended warranty. How should the two warranties be accounted for?
choices: Both are separate performance obligations with revenue deferred
Both are accrued as warranty expense with no revenue deferral
The extended warranty is accrued as an expense and the standard warranty is a performance obligation
The standard warranty is accrued as a cost under ASC 460 and the extended warranty is a separate performance obligation
exp: An assurance-type warranty that only promises the product meets specifications is accrued as a cost, while a warranty the customer can buy separately is a service-type warranty and a distinct performance obligation (ASC 606-10-55-30 through 55-35). Treating both as expense accruals is the most common error.

q: On January 1, a company sells a machine bundled with a three-year extended service-type warranty for $1,080. Standalone selling prices are $1,000 for the machine and $200 for the warranty. Warranty revenue is recognized straight-line from the date of sale. How much revenue should the company recognize in the year of sale?
exp: Warranty allocation = $1,080 x $200 / $1,200 = $180 and machine = $900; revenue in Year 1 = $900 + ($180 / 3) = $960. Recognizing the entire $1,080 at sale ignores that the warranty is satisfied over time.

q: A company grants a franchisee the right to use its trade name and brand for 10 years in exchange for an upfront fee. The company will continue activities that significantly affect the brand. How should the upfront fee be recognized?
choices: Over time over the license term, because it is a right to access symbolic intellectual property
At the point in time the license is granted, because it is a right to use functional intellectual property
When cash is received
Only at the end of the license term
exp: A brand or trade name is symbolic IP, and a license to it is a right to access recognized over time (ASC 606-10-55-58 through 55-63). Point-in-time recognition applies to functional IP such as completed software or film.

q: A software company licenses functional IP and receives a royalty equal to 5% of the licensee's sales of products incorporating the software. How should the company recognize the royalty revenue?
choices: Estimate total royalties and recognize them when the license is transferred
Recognize royalties only when cash is received
Recognize royalties at the later of when the licensee's sales occur or the related performance obligation is satisfied
Recognize royalties evenly over the contract term
exp: The sales- or usage-based royalty exception in ASC 606-10-55-65 prohibits estimating these royalties up front; they are recognized at the later of the subsequent sale or satisfaction of the obligation. Estimating total royalties under the general variable consideration guidance is the trap.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the criteria that must be met for a seller to recognize revenue in a bill-and-hold arrangement?
choices: The reason for the arrangement is substantive
The product is identified separately as belonging to the customer
The product is ready for physical transfer to the customer
The customer has paid the full purchase price in advance
exp: ASC 606-10-55-83 requires a substantive reason, separate identification, readiness for physical transfer, and that the seller cannot use the product or direct it to another customer. Payment in advance is not a requirement.

q: A consignor shipped goods costing $60,000 to a consignee. During the year, the consignee sold 40% of the goods to end customers for $50,000 and kept a 10% commission. The consignor is the principal. How much revenue should the consignor recognize?
exp: A consignor recognizes revenue only when goods are sold to end customers, and as principal it reports the gross sales of $50,000 with a $5,000 commission expense. Reporting $45,000 nets the commission against revenue, which is incorrect for a principal.

q: A retailer sold $100,000 of gift cards during the year and expects 10% to never be redeemed, based on reliable history. Customers redeemed $45,000 of gift cards during the year. Breakage is recognized in proportion to the pattern of redemption. How much revenue should the retailer recognize this year related to the gift cards?
exp: Expected redemptions are $90,000; $45,000 redeemed is 50% of that, so 50% of expected breakage ($10,000) is recognized: $45,000 + $5,000 = $50,000 (ASC 606-10-55-48). Recognizing all $10,000 of breakage immediately gives the $55,000 trap.

q: A retailer's sales were $100,000 this period, and customers earned 10,000 loyalty points, each redeemable for a $1 discount on future purchases. The retailer expects 80% of points to be redeemed. Points are a material right. How much revenue should be recognized on the sales this period?
exp: The points' standalone selling price is $8,000 (10,000 x $1 x 80%), so revenue for goods = $100,000 x $100,000 / $108,000 = $92,593, and $7,407 is deferred. Subtracting the $8,000 directly ($92,000) skips the relative standalone selling price allocation.

q: A beverage maker sold $200,000 of products to a grocery chain and paid the chain $10,000 in slotting fees for shelf space. The maker receives no distinct good or service in exchange for the fees. How much revenue should the beverage maker recognize?
choices: $200,000, with $10,000 of selling expense
$200,000, with $10,000 recorded as a prepaid asset
exp: Consideration payable to a customer that is not for a distinct good or service reduces the transaction price (ASC 606-10-32-25), so revenue is $190,000. Recording it as selling expense with $200,000 of revenue is the trap.

q: A contract calls for 120 distinct units at $100 each. After 60 units are delivered, the contract is modified to add 30 more units at $80 each, which is not the standalone selling price. The remaining goods are distinct from those already transferred. At what price per unit should revenue be recognized for the remaining 90 units?
choices: $100 for the original units and $80 for the added units
exp: Because the added goods are not priced at standalone selling price but the remaining goods are distinct, the modification is treated as termination of the old contract and creation of a new one: (60 x $100 + 30 x $80) / 90 = $93.33. Keeping separate prices applies only when the added goods are priced at standalone selling price.

q: Under ASC 606, when should an entity present a receivable rather than a contract asset for its right to consideration?
choices: When the right to consideration is unconditional, requiring only the passage of time
When the entity has satisfied any performance obligation
When an invoice has been prepared, regardless of remaining obligations
When the customer has signed the contract
exp: A receivable is an unconditional right to consideration; if the right depends on something other than the passage of time, such as future performance, it is a contract asset. Satisfying one obligation while payment still depends on another produces a contract asset, not a receivable.

q: Which situation would NOT, by itself, cause a performance obligation to be satisfied over time under ASC 606?
choices: The customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits as the entity performs
The entity's performance creates an asset the customer controls as it is created
The entity's performance creates an asset with an alternative use to the entity
The entity's performance creates an asset with no alternative use and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for performance to date
exp: The third over-time criterion requires both no alternative use and an enforceable right to payment (ASC 606-10-25-27); an asset with an alternative use fails it. The other situations each satisfy one of the over-time criteria.

q: During the year, a company classified a component as held for sale; the disposal represents a strategic shift with a major effect on operations. The component had an operating loss of $300,000 for the year, and its carrying amount of $2,000,000 exceeds its fair value less cost to sell of $1,700,000. The tax rate is 25%. What amount should be reported as loss from discontinued operations, net of tax?
exp: The operating loss and the $300,000 write-down to fair value less cost to sell are both reported in discontinued operations: ($300,000 + $300,000) x (1 - 25%) = $450,000 (ASC 205-20). Omitting the tax effect gives $600,000, and omitting the write-down gives $225,000.

q: Which disposal is most likely to be reported as a discontinued operation under ASC 205-20?
choices: Sale of a major geographic segment that represents a strategic shift with a major effect on operations and results
Sale of one of 40 retail stores in a region the company continues to serve
Discontinuing one minor product line within a product group
Sale of excess manufacturing equipment
exp: A disposal qualifies only if it represents a strategic shift that has, or will have, a major effect on operations and financial results, such as exiting a major geographic area. Selling one store or a minor product line typically does not meet that threshold.

q: How should a material gain that is both unusual in nature and infrequent in occurrence be presented on the income statement under current U.S. GAAP?
choices: As an extraordinary item, net of tax, after discontinued operations
As a separate line item within income from continuing operations, before tax
In other comprehensive income
As an adjustment to beginning retained earnings
exp: ASU 2015-01 eliminated extraordinary items; unusual or infrequent items are reported separately within income from continuing operations on a pretax basis or disclosed in the notes (ASC 225-20). Net-of-tax extraordinary presentation is no longer permitted.

q: A company had net income of $1,000,000. It has 10,000 shares of $100 par, 6% cumulative preferred stock outstanding; no dividends were declared this year. It had 200,000 common shares outstanding on January 1 and issued 60,000 common shares on July 1. What is basic earnings per share?
exp: Cumulative preferred dividends are deducted whether or not declared: ($1,000,000 - $60,000) / (200,000 + 60,000 x 6/12) = $940,000 / 230,000 = $4.09 (ASC 260). Ignoring the undeclared preferred dividend gives $4.35.

q: A company had 100,000 common shares outstanding on January 1. It issued 20,000 shares for cash on April 1 and distributed a 10% stock dividend on October 1. What is the weighted-average number of shares for basic EPS?
exp: Stock dividends are applied retroactively to all shares outstanding before them: 100,000 x 1.10 + 20,000 x 1.10 x 9/12 = 110,000 + 16,500 = 126,500. Failing to restate the April issuance for the dividend gives 125,000.

q: A company had net income of $500,000 and 100,000 common shares outstanding all year. It also had $1,000,000 of 6% bonds outstanding all year, convertible into 20,000 common shares. The tax rate is 25%. What is diluted earnings per share?
exp: Under the if-converted method, add back after-tax interest of $60,000 x 75% = $45,000: ($500,000 + $45,000) / 120,000 = $4.54; the bonds are dilutive because $45,000 / 20,000 = $2.25 is below basic EPS of $5.00. Adding back pretax interest gives the $4.67 trap.

q: A company changes from the double-declining-balance to the straight-line depreciation method for its existing equipment. How should this change be accounted for?
choices: Retrospectively, by restating prior periods
Prospectively, as a change in estimate effected by a change in accounting principle
As a cumulative-effect adjustment in current-period net income
As a correction of an error
exp: ASC 250 treats a change in depreciation method as a change in accounting estimate effected by a change in principle, applied prospectively. Retrospective restatement is required for most other changes in principle, which is why it is the tempting choice.

q: A company receives a $50,000 nonrefundable deposit from a customer under an agreement for which collectibility of the remaining consideration is not probable, so the contract does not meet the ASC 606 criteria. The company has not transferred goods and continues to have obligations under the agreement. How should the deposit be recorded?
choices: As revenue when received, because it is nonrefundable
As a reduction of accounts receivable
As a liability until the contract criteria are met or another ASC 606 event allows revenue recognition
As deferred revenue recognized straight-line over the contract term
exp: When a contract fails the existence criteria, consideration received is a liability until the criteria are met, or the entity has no remaining obligations and has received substantially all consideration, or the contract is terminated (ASC 606-10-25-7 and 25-8). Being nonrefundable alone does not permit revenue recognition.

q: A company sells equipment to a customer for $500,000 and holds a call right to repurchase the equipment in two years for $550,000. How should the company account for the transaction?
choices: As a financing arrangement, because the repurchase price exceeds the original selling price
As a sale with revenue of $500,000 recognized at delivery
As a lease, because the repurchase price exceeds the selling price
As a sale with a right of return
exp: When the seller has a call right, the customer never obtains control, and a repurchase price at or above the original selling price makes it a financing arrangement (ASC 606-10-55-68). Lease treatment applies only if the repurchase price is below the original selling price.
